## What would a collaborator need?

We use the **FAIR** principles to document the
`HealthWellbeing` teaching snapshot and assess what software can
discover about it. The table gives one question to ask for each
principle [@gofair-principles].

| Principle | Ask | Example for this dataset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Findable** | Can someone locate and identify it? | A named record with a stable identifier and searchable metadata. |
| **Accessible** | How can someone retrieve it, and on what terms? | A working download link with a statement of the access terms, or clear instructions for requesting access. |
| **Interoperable** | Can people and software interpret its structure? | Use shared metadata terms such as Schema.org and describe the variables and their units. |
| **Reusable** | Can someone judge whether it suits their project? | Explain the source, the unit of observation, and the licence. |

## Describe the snapshot with dataspice {#create-fair-metadata}

Four prepared CSV files under
`data/metadata/health-wellbeing/` record the title and licence, creator,
download link, and variables. `n` in `attributes.csv` (line 4) says
that each row of the data describes **one study** and `n` is the sample
size within that study. The teaching snapshot has 29 rows and five
variables [@healthwellbeing].

```{r health-dataspice-export-edit, eval = FALSE}
file.edit(
  file.path("data", "metadata", "health-wellbeing", "attributes.csv")
)
```

*dataspice* combines the CSV files into a Schema.org JSON-LD record
[@dataspice]. The excerpt shows the title, licence, download link, and variables, so you can see that its meaning and unit survive the
export.

source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
use_workshop_book_outputs()

```{r health-dataspice-export, eval = TRUE}
source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
source_dir <- file.path("data", "metadata", "health-wellbeing")

metadata_dir <- file.path(workshop_output_dir(), "metadata")
dir.create(metadata_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

templates <- file.path(
  source_dir, c("biblio.csv", "creators.csv", "access.csv", "attributes.csv")
)
stopifnot(all(file.copy(templates, metadata_dir, overwrite = TRUE)))
dataspice::write_spice(path = metadata_dir)

record <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path(metadata_dir, "dataspice.json"))
excerpt <- record[c("name", "license", "distribution")]
excerpt$variableMeasured <- Filter(
  function(variable) variable$name == "n", record$variableMeasured
)
jsonlite::toJSON(excerpt, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)
```

This record describes the [verified teaching file](00_preparation.qmd#preparation-data), detailing the `n` variable. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## HealthWellbeing JSON-LD

```{r health-jsonld-record, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = TRUE}
metadata_file <- file.path("data", "metadata", "health-wellbeing", "dataspice.json")
cat(c("```json", readLines(metadata_file, warn = FALSE), "```"), sep = "\n")
```
:::

## Assess the snapshot with rfair {#assess-fair-metadata}

*rfair* takes a URL or persistent identifier and applies a set of tests
to the metadata it can retrieve [@rfair]. 

First, assess the `HealthWellbeing.rda` file:

```{r health-rfair-baseline, eval = TRUE}
metadata_file <- file.path("data", "metadata", "health-wellbeing", "dataspice.json")
metadata <- jsonlite::read_json(metadata_file)
snapshot_url <- metadata$distribution[[1L]]$contentUrl
baseline <- rfair::assess_fair(
  snapshot_url, metric_version = "0.8", timeout = 6, max_time = 30
)
baseline
```

We will next assess the JSON-D file:

```{r health-rfair-enriched, eval = TRUE}
metadata_url <- paste0(
  "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r@",
  "c08e0dc036e46e89376536a87ad279db61374f7e",
  "/data/metadata/health-wellbeing/dataspice.json"
)
enriched <- rfair::assess_fair(
  snapshot_url,
  metric_version = "0.8",
  metadata_service_endpoint = metadata_url,
  metadata_service_type = "schema_org",
  timeout = 6,
  max_time = 30
)
enriched
```

And follow up with a comparison of the original evaluation against this new evaluation:

```{r health-rfair-comparison, eval = TRUE}
comparison <- rfair::fair_compare(baseline, enriched)
metrics <- c("FsF-F1-02MD", "FsF-A1-01M", "FsF-I1-01M", "FsF-R1.1-01M")
comparison[comparison$metric_identifier %in% metrics,
           c("metric_identifier", "status_a", "status_b")]
```

One metric from each principle shows what changed and what
stayed the same.

| Metric | Download URL alone | With the JSON-LD supplied |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Persistent identifier (`FsF-F1-02MD`) | Fail | Fail |
| Access information in metadata (`FsF-A1-01M`) | Fail | Fail |
| Formal language for metadata (`FsF-I1-01M`) | Fail | Pass |
| Licence in metadata (`FsF-R1.1-01M`) | Fail | Pass |

The file downloaded successfully in both
runs, yet the access check (`FsF-A1-01M`) failed both times. Why? What would you add
to the public record so a reader knows how to get the file?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## One possible answer

This metric looks for access information in the metadata. A working
link shows that the assessor could download the file at that moment.
It does not tell a reader whether anyone can download it, whether
they need to sign in, or whether they must request approval.

For this snapshot, a statement such as "Public download, no sign-in
required" beside the URL would answer the question. Schema.org has
`isAccessibleForFree` and `conditionsOfAccess` properties for this.
For a restricted dataset, the record could say who may access the data
and how to request it. Rerun the assessment to check whether a
particular metric version recognises the statement.
:::

## Checkpoint {#metadata-checkpoint}

The record now says what the data mean and how to get them. It does
not say which version of the data produced a given result. Next, we
identify that version.
[Data and model versioning](04_versioning.qmd)
